sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is a partially articulated skeleton of an eight-year-old subadult measuring 2.77 meters in length.
This immature individual is estimated to have weighed between 24 and 30 kilograms.
Its forelimbs are shorter than those of Jurassic relatives but longer than Late Cretaceous forms, showing an extended thumb and shortened digits that indicate a loss of grasping function.
Analysis of intestinal contents detected bone-derived material, suggesting a carnivorous diet.
This animal fills a seventy-million-year evolutionary gap by displaying intermediate features between early and late alvarezsaurids.
Discovered in 2009, the fossil was first displayed in Japan in 2012 under the unofficial name Wulatesaurus before being formally named Bannykus wulatensis in 2018.
The remains were found in the Bayin-Gobi Formation of Inner Mongolia, China.
Researchers suggest the forelimbs were capable of generalized motions used for various digging styles.
Analysis indicates that alvarezsaurian evolution was modular, with forelimbs modifying before hindlimbs.
The genus Bannykus is monotypic, containing only the species Bannykus wulatensis.
Phylogenetic analysis confirms a basal position for Alvarezsauria within Maniraptora.
The animal lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically between 124 and 113 million years ago in the Barremian stage.
Bannykus originates from Asia, suggesting the group evolved there before spreading to other continents.
It is debated whether alvarezsaurian species appeared on other continents via migration or allopatric speciation, with recent analysis favoring migration.
